name: Carbamazepine (Tegretol)
summary: Antiseizure drug with mood-stabilizing effects, used as an alternative mood stabilizer for bipolar mania and mixed episodes. Powerful but requires careful monitoring for rare, serious blood, liver, sodium, and skin reactions.
description: Carbamazepine is an antiseizure medicine that also acts as a mood stabilizer. In psychiatry, it’s mainly used for bipolar disorder—especially hypomania, mild to moderate mania, and mixed episodes—when first-line options like lithium, valproate, or atypical antipsychotics are not tolerated or have not worked well. It can also be continued longer term in some people to reduce the risk of future mood episodes. Because carbamazepine can, in rare cases, cause life-threatening skin reactions, serious blood problems, liver injury, and low sodium, it should only be used with regular lab monitoring and good follow-up.
patient_summary: Carbamazepine (brand name Tegretol, plus several others) is a medicine that treats seizures and can also act as a mood stabilizer. In mental health care it’s mostly used for bipolar disorder, especially for hypomania, mild to moderate mania, and “mixed” episodes where mood is both high and low at the same time. It can calm racing thoughts, irritability, and agitation over days to weeks. The trade-off is that carbamazepine has some rare but serious risks involving your skin, blood cells, liver, and salt (sodium) level. Because of that, doctors order regular blood tests and tell patients to report rashes, fevers, or signs of infection right away.

primary_indications: Bipolar I Disorder – acute hypomania, mild to moderate mania, and mixed episodes (alternative agent)
Bipolar Disorder – maintenance after successful acute treatment (off-label, alternative agent)
Focal (partial) onset and generalized tonic–clonic seizures
Trigeminal or glossopharyngeal neuralgia (neuropathic facial pain)

linked_conditions.context: Used as an alternative to lithium, valproate, or atypical antipsychotics in acute hypomania, mild–moderate mania, or mixed episodes, especially when those options are not tolerated or ineffective.
Sometimes continued as a maintenance mood stabilizer after a good response in an acute episode; long-term evidence is weaker than for lithium or valproate, so it is usually not a first choice.
Approved antiseizure medication for focal and generalized tonic–clonic seizures; relevant in psychiatric patients with comorbid epilepsy.
Standard treatment for trigeminal neuralgia; may be useful when severe facial pain and mood symptoms co-occur.

contraindications: History of serious hypersensitivity to carbamazepine, other tricyclic-related drugs, or any component of the product
Existing bone marrow suppression or serious blood disorder (eg, aplastic anemia, agranulocytosis)
Positive HLA-B*1502 test in at-risk Asian ancestry when alternatives are available (high risk of Stevens–Johnson syndrome/toxic epidermal necrolysis)
Use with or within 14 days of a monoamine oxidase inhibitor (MAOI)
Concomitant use of nefazodone, delavirdine, or other contraindicated CYP3A4 substrates
Significant atrioventricular (AV) conduction block or serious conduction disease (per Canadian and other labeling)
Hepatic porphyria or serious active liver disease (per Canadian labeling)

efficacy_response.metric: Clinical response in acute bipolar mania (≥50% improvement in mania scores)
efficacy_response.comparison_data: Placebo response around 20–25% in large randomized trials of extended-release carbamazepine.
efficacy_response.patient_text: In modern bipolar studies, roughly 4 out of 10 people with acute mania have their symptoms cut in half or more on carbamazepine after a few weeks, compared with about 2 out of 10 on placebo. It generally works about as well as other classic mood stabilizers, but is often reserved as an alternative because of its side-effect profile and many drug interactions.
efficacy_response.citation_tag: Weisler 2004; related RCTs of carbamazepine XR in acute mania

pharmacokinetics.absorption: Slow and somewhat variable from the gut; food can modestly increase exposure.
pharmacokinetics.onset: Sedation and dizziness can appear in days; meaningful mood stabilization often takes 1–3 weeks at a therapeutic level.
pharmacokinetics.peak_plasma: Immediate-release tablets about 4–5 hours; suspension around 1.5 hours; extended-release tablets/capsules 4–12 hours after steady dosing.
pharmacokinetics.half_life: Highly variable; initially long (about 25–65 hours) then typically 12–17 hours in adults once autoinduction is complete.
pharmacokinetics.duration_IR: Requires 2–4 divided doses per day for stable levels.
pharmacokinetics.duration_XR: Formulated for twice-daily dosing with smoother 12-hour coverage.
pharmacokinetics.metabolism: Extensively metabolized in the liver, mainly via CYP3A4, to an active epoxide metabolite; carbamazepine strongly induces multiple CYP enzymes and transporters, lowering levels of many other medications.
pharmacokinetics.excretion: Primarily via the kidneys as metabolites, with a smaller portion in feces.
pharmacokinetics.food_effect: Grapefruit and grapefruit juice can significantly increase carbamazepine levels and should be avoided.

sections.heading: What It’s Used For
sections.text: Carbamazepine is an antiseizure medication that also acts as a mood stabilizer. In psychiatry it is usually considered an alternative option, not a first-line mood stabilizer.
items: {link:condition:bipolar-i-disorder:Bipolar I Disorder}: hypomania, mild to moderate mania, or mixed episodes (alternative to lithium or valproate)
Maintenance mood stabilization after a good acute response (off-label, alternative choice)
{link:condition:focal-onset-seizures:Focal and generalized tonic–clonic seizures} when epilepsy and mood symptoms coexist
{link:condition:trigeminal-neuralgia:Trigeminal or glossopharyngeal neuralgia} (severe facial pain) in people also being treated for mood symptoms
off_label: Bipolar major depression (data mixed; rarely a first-choice treatment)
Adjunctive use in complex mood or aggression disorders in specialist settings

sections.heading: What People Often Notice
sections.intro: Individual responses vary, but these are common patterns when carbamazepine is used as a mood stabilizer:

quotes: My thoughts weren’t racing as much, but I felt a bit slowed down.
The irritability eased up, though I was more tired than usual.
I felt less ‘amped’ and more level, but also somewhat groggy.
I felt wobbly and light-headed at the beginning.
It helped my mood but made me want daytime naps.
The dizziness improved after dose adjustments, but didn’t completely go away.
items.note: Sedation, dizziness, and feeling unsteady are very common, especially during dose increases or at higher doses.

quotes: My brain felt slower and it was harder to multitask.
I sometimes lost my train of thought mid-sentence.
Work was doable, but I felt mentally ‘thicker’ than before.
items.note: Mild cognitive slowing is common and can be dose-limiting for some people.

quotes: I developed a painful rash and had to stop the medicine quickly.
A blood test picked up low counts before I felt sick.
My sodium was low on a lab test, so we adjusted the plan.
items.note: Dangerous skin reactions, blood problems, liver injury, and very low sodium are rare but serious—monitoring is key.

sections.heading: How Fast It Works
sections.text: Carbamazepine is not an instant “rescue” medication. It needs time to reach a steady level and for the brain to adjust.
key_points: First few days: Sleepiness, dizziness, and mild stomach upset are common while your body adapts.
1–2 weeks: Many people notice some calming of mania, irritability, or agitation.
2–4 weeks: Full benefit for acute mania or mixed episodes is often seen; doses and blood levels may still need fine-tuning.
Formulations: Extended-release forms give smoother coverage and are usually taken twice daily; immediate-release forms often need 2–4 doses per day.
Autoinduction: The liver speeds up carbamazepine metabolism over the first 3–5 weeks, which can lower levels and sometimes requires dose increases.

sections.heading: Critical Safety Information
sections.highlight: Severe skin reactions and serious blood problems are rare but can be life-threatening. New rash, fever, mouth sores, or signs of infection need urgent medical review.
sections.black_box: Carbamazepine can cause very serious skin reactions (Stevens–Johnson syndrome and toxic epidermal necrolysis), especially in people with the HLA-B*1502 gene variant common in some Asian populations. It can also cause life-threatening blood disorders such as aplastic anemia and agranulocytosis. In at-risk groups, genetic screening and regular blood tests are strongly recommended.
other: Serious skin reactions: Painful rash, blisters, skin peeling, or sores on the lips, mouth, or eyes can signal a medical emergency. The medicine is usually stopped permanently if this happens.

Genetic risk (HLA-B*1502 and HLA-A*3101): In some people of Asian or certain other ancestries, these gene variants greatly increase the risk of severe skin reactions. Testing is often advised before starting if ancestry suggests higher risk.

Blood problems: Carbamazepine can lower white blood cells and platelets, and rarely cause aplastic anemia or agranulocytosis. Warning signs include fever, sore throat, mouth ulcers, frequent infections, unexplained bruising, or pinpoint red spots.

Liver injury: Can cause mild liver test changes or, rarely, severe hepatitis or liver failure, sometimes as part of a multisystem reaction (DRESS). Symptoms include fatigue, nausea, dark urine, yellowing of the eyes or skin, or pain under the right ribs.

Hyponatremia and SIADH: Carbamazepine can lower blood sodium, leading to headache, confusion, nausea, falls, seizures, or extreme sleepiness. Older adults and people on diuretics or SSRIs are especially vulnerable.
Cardiac conduction issues: In people with heart disease or conduction problems, carbamazepine can worsen AV block or heart failure.

Suicidal thoughts: Like other antiseizure drugs, carbamazepine has been linked to a small increase in suicidal thinking. Mood and suicidality should be checked regularly, especially early in treatment.

Drug interactions: Carbamazepine strongly induces liver enzymes, which can lower levels of many drugs (including hormonal birth control, some antipsychotics, antidepressants, and other antiseizure medicines).
Seizure type: It can worsen absence or some other generalized seizure types and should not be used for those conditions.
Stopping suddenly: Abrupt discontinuation can trigger seizures, rebound mood episodes, or withdrawal-like symptoms; tapers are usually gradual unless there is a serious reaction.
patient_counseling: Call your clinician or seek urgent care right away for any new painful or blistering rash, fever, mouth sores, or unexplained bruising.
Expect routine blood tests to monitor blood counts, liver and kidney function, sodium, and carbamazepine levels—this is standard safety care.
Avoid grapefruit and grapefruit juice—they can raise carbamazepine levels and increase side effects.
Use reliable contraception if pregnancy is possible, and know that carbamazepine can weaken many hormonal birth control methods.
Always check with a clinician or pharmacist before adding, stopping, or changing any other medicines or supplements.
Do not stop carbamazepine suddenly unless you are told to stop immediately for a serious reaction. Most people come off the medication slowly with medical guidance.

sections.heading: Side Effects
sections.summary: Common effects include drowsiness, dizziness, and mental “slowing.” Rare but serious effects involve the skin, blood cells, liver, sodium, and mood.
plain_language_list: Sleepiness or feeling generally slowed down
Dizziness or feeling off-balance (higher fall risk)
Mild stomach upset, nausea, or constipation
Thinking and memory feeling a bit foggy or slower
Rarely: severe rash, fever, mouth sores, easy bruising, yellowing of eyes or skin, confusion, or seizures due to low sodium

common.incidence: Very common, especially during dose increases
common.patient_note: Often strongest in the first week or two, or right after a dose change. Taking doses with food or shifting more of the dose to evening can help in some people.
You may feel wobbly or “tipsy,” especially if you stand quickly. Use handrails, avoid ladders, and be cautious with driving until you know how you respond.
Vision changes can appear as the dose goes up. They often improve with dose adjustment or time. Do not drive or run machinery if your vision is affected.
People often describe feeling less sharp or taking longer to process information. If this interferes with daily life, your team may adjust the dose or consider another medication.

common.incidence: Varies; often mild and only seen on labs
common.patient_note: Symptoms can include headache, nausea, confusion, or feeling very unsteady. Older adults and people on diuretics or SSRIs need especially careful sodium monitoring.
Many rashes are mild, but it’s impossible to be sure without an exam. Any new rash should be reviewed quickly, and a painful or blistering rash is an emergency.

serious: Stevens–Johnson syndrome and toxic epidermal necrolysis: painful rash, blisters, skin peeling, eye involvement, and fever; more common in some genetic backgrounds and requires emergency care.
Aplastic anemia and agranulocytosis: near-complete shutdown of bone marrow or severe loss of white cells, causing infections, bleeding, and extreme fatigue.
Severe liver injury, including liver failure or vanishing bile duct syndrome: yellow eyes or skin, dark urine, intense fatigue, itching, or abdominal pain.
Severe hyponatremia and SIADH: confusion, seizures, falls, or reduced consciousness from very low sodium levels.
Multiorgan hypersensitivity (DRESS): fever, rash, swollen lymph nodes, liver or kidney inflammation, and blood changes.
Cardiac conduction block or serious arrhythmias: fainting, palpitations, or worsening heart failure in susceptible people.
Suicidal thoughts or behavior: new or worsening depression, anxiety, agitation, or suicidal thinking, especially in the first months of treatment.
Severe neurotoxicity or overdose: marked drowsiness, confusion, slurred speech, loss of coordination, abnormal eye movements, low blood pressure, or seizures.

sections.heading: Important Drug and Substance Interactions
sections.intro: Carbamazepine interacts with many other medicines because it strongly affects liver enzymes and is also affected by them.

items.with: Hormonal contraceptives (pill, patch, ring, some implants)
items.risk: Carbamazepine speeds up hormone breakdown, making birth control less effective.
items.action: Use a backup non-hormonal method (eg, copper IUD, condoms) or another reliable option not as affected by enzyme induction.

items.with: Other antiseizure drugs and mood stabilizers (eg, valproate, lamotrigine, phenytoin, phenobarbital)
items.risk: Levels of both carbamazepine and the other drugs can go up or down, affecting seizure control, mood, and side effects.
items.action: Dose adjustments and blood-level checks are often needed when combining these medications.

items.risk: Carbamazepine can lower levels of many antidepressants and antipsychotics, and some can raise carbamazepine or epoxide levels.
items.action: Prescribers may need to adjust doses and monitor for loss of effect or increased side effects.

items.with: Strong CYP3A4 inhibitors (eg, some azole antifungals, macrolide antibiotics, certain antivirals, grapefruit products)
items.risk: These can sharply increase carbamazepine levels, leading to toxicity.
items.action: Often avoided; if necessary, careful monitoring and dose adjustments are required. Grapefruit juice is generally avoided.

items.with: Alcohol and other sedating medicines (benzodiazepines, sleep aids, opioids)
items.risk: Additive sedation, poor coordination, breathing problems, and overdose risk.
items.action: Limit or avoid alcohol; discuss any sedating medications with your prescriber.

items.risk: Higher chance of low sodium and SIADH.
items.action: More frequent sodium checks and careful review of symptoms such as headache, confusion, or falls.

sections.heading: Stopping Carbamazepine Safely
sections.text: Outside of serious allergic or toxic reactions, carbamazepine is usually reduced slowly rather than stopped suddenly.
key_points: For bipolar disorder, coming off too quickly can trigger a return of mania, hypomania, or depression.
For people with seizures, abrupt discontinuation can cause seizure worsening or prolonged seizures (status epilepticus).
Typical tapers reduce the total daily dose by about 10–25% at a time, spaced over weeks to months.
The taper schedule depends on your condition, how long you’ve been taking carbamazepine, your current dose, and your past relapse risk.
If a severe rash, blood problem, liver injury, or very low sodium occurs, the medicine may need to be stopped more rapidly under close medical supervision.

sections.heading: Dosing (Adults – Psychiatric Use)
sections.text: Dosing is individualized and titrated slowly, guided by symptoms, side effects, and blood levels.

adult.bipolar_acute_mania_initial: 100–400 mg per day by mouth, divided into 2–4 doses depending on formulation.
adult.bipolar_acute_mania_titration: Increase by up to 200 mg per day every 1–4 days as tolerated.
adult.bipolar_acute_mania_usual: 600–1,200 mg per day divided into 2–4 doses; some patients need up to 1,600–1,800 mg per day under specialist care.
adult.maintenance_bipolar: Continue the lowest effective dose that stabilized the acute episode; adjust based on mood and blood levels.
adult.elderly: Start lower (for example, 100–200 mg per day) and titrate slowly; monitor closely for dizziness, falls, confusion, and low sodium.
adult.hepatic_impairment: Use with caution and start at the lowest possible dose in mild impairment; avoid in severe liver disease when possible.
adult.renal_impairment: No routine starting-dose change, but monitor drug and metabolite levels and side effects in moderate to severe kidney disease.

sections.simple_explanation: Most people start on a low dose of carbamazepine and increase gradually. Immediate-release tablets often need 2–4 doses per day, while extended-release forms are usually taken twice daily. Blood tests help confirm that the level is in a helpful range without being too high.

sections.heading: Pregnancy, Breastfeeding, and Special Groups
sections.text: Carbamazepine can be used in people who are pregnant or breastfeeding, but only after carefully weighing risks and benefits and often with extra monitoring.
sections.pregnancy: Carbamazepine is associated with a higher risk of certain birth defects (such as spina bifida and some heart and facial problems) compared with the general population, though risk appears lower than with some other antiseizure medicines. At the same time, uncontrolled bipolar disorder or seizures can be dangerous for both parent and baby. Ideally, pregnancy planning includes discussion of folic acid, safer alternatives if appropriate, and how to monitor you and the fetus if carbamazepine is continued.
sections.lactation: Carbamazepine and its active metabolite pass into breast milk in modest amounts. Most studies show normal development in breastfed infants, but rare cases of sedation, poor feeding, or liver test changes have been reported. If you breastfeed while taking carbamazepine, your baby’s pediatrician should monitor for sleepiness, feeding difficulties, weight gain, jaundice, and developmental milestones.
sections.pediatrics: Commonly used for epilepsy and neuralgia in children; less commonly as a mood stabilizer. Children may be more vulnerable to certain seizure-type worsening and severe skin reactions. Dosing is weight-based and families should be educated about rash and the need for lab monitoring.
sections.geriatrics: Older adults are more prone to dizziness, falls, confusion, low sodium, and heart conduction problems. Guidelines flag carbamazepine as potentially inappropriate in many older patients unless there is a strong reason. If used, start low, go slow, and monitor closely.
sections.hepatic: Because carbamazepine is metabolized in the liver and can injure the liver, it should be avoided or used very cautiously in people with significant hepatic impairment.
sections.renal: No standard starting-dose change is needed in mild to moderate kidney disease, but monitoring of levels and side effects is important, especially with more severe impairment.

sections.heading: Monitoring and Follow-Up
items: Before starting: CBC with differential and platelets; liver and kidney function; electrolytes (especially sodium); pregnancy test when relevant.
Genetic testing: In people with Asian or certain other ancestries, consider HLA-B*1502 (and often HLA-A*3101) testing before starting, where available.
Drug levels: Check carbamazepine levels during titration, after dose changes, after adding interacting drugs, and periodically during maintenance.
CBC and liver tests: Repeat regularly, especially in the first several months, to catch emerging blood or liver problems.
Sodium: Monitor more frequently in older adults, those on diuretics or SSRIs/SNRIs, and anyone with prior low sodium.
Psychiatric status: Track mood, sleep, energy, and suicidal ideation routinely, especially during the first 1–3 months.
Function: Ask about work/school performance, relationships, and daily functioning to judge whether benefits outweigh side effects.
Pregnancy and breastfeeding: In pregnant patients, consider more frequent drug levels and fetal monitoring; in breastfeeding patients, monitor infants for sedation, feeding, and growth.

sections.heading: Formulations
sections.text: All psychiatric uses of carbamazepine are oral. Different formulations affect how quickly the drug is absorbed and how often it needs to be taken.
items: Immediate-release tablets and chewable tablets: Usually taken 2–4 times per day with food.
Oral suspension: Absorbed more quickly; generally needs 3–4 doses per day and careful conversion from tablet doses.
Extended-release (XR) tablets: Swallowed whole, usually twice daily; provide smoother levels and may reduce peak-related side effects.
Extended-release capsules (eg, Carbatrol, Equetro): Contain beads for immediate and delayed release; can sometimes be opened and sprinkled on soft food as directed by the product label.

sections.heading: How It Works in the Brain
sections.text: Carbamazepine mainly works by blocking voltage-gated sodium channels on overactive neurons. This helps “steady” electrical activity in the brain, which reduces seizures and seems to damp down the overactivation that contributes to mania and mixed states. It also has mild anticholinergic and antidiuretic effects and shares a three-ring (tricyclic) structure with some older antidepressants, which likely contributes to both its mood effects and side-effect profile.

sections.heading: Where It Fits in Treatment
sections.text: For bipolar disorder, carbamazepine is usually an alternative mood stabilizer rather than a first-line choice. Lithium, valproate, and atypical antipsychotics typically come first because they have more robust evidence and fewer complex interactions. Carbamazepine becomes more attractive when someone cannot tolerate first-line agents, has comorbid focal epilepsy or trigeminal neuralgia, or has a strong past response to carbamazepine. Because of its serious possible side effects and many interactions, it is best used by clinicians experienced with mood stabilizers, with regular lab monitoring and careful follow-up.

seo.title: Carbamazepine (Tegretol): Mood Stabilizer for Bipolar Mania – Uses, Dosing, Side Effects & Monitoring
seo.description: Carbamazepine (Tegretol) as an alternative mood stabilizer for bipolar mania and mixed episodes: how it works, typical dosing, serious skin and blood risks, lab monitoring, and key pregnancy and breastfeeding considerations.

editorial.reviewStatement: Content focused on psychiatric use of carbamazepine and intended for formal medical review against current FDA labeling, bipolar disorder guidelines, and contemporary safety and monitoring data.

faqs.q: What is carbamazepine used for in psychiatry?
faqs.a: In mental health, carbamazepine is mainly used as a mood stabilizer for bipolar disorder, especially for hypomania, mild to moderate mania, and mixed episodes. It is usually considered when lithium, valproate, or atypical antipsychotics are not tolerated, are unsafe, or have not worked well. It may then be continued long term to help prevent future mood episodes.

faqs.q: How long does carbamazepine take to work for bipolar mania?
faqs.a: Carbamazepine does not work instantly. Side effects like sleepiness and dizziness may appear in the first few days, but meaningful improvement in mania or mixed symptoms usually takes 1–2 weeks, with full benefit often taking 3–4 weeks at a therapeutic dose and blood level. Because the drug speeds up its own metabolism over the first few weeks, doses sometimes need to be adjusted during this period.

faqs.q: Why do I need blood tests on carbamazepine?
faqs.a: Routine blood tests are an essential safety part of carbamazepine treatment. They help check your blood counts, liver and kidney function, sodium level, and carbamazepine level. This allows your team to detect rare but serious problems—like very low white cells, low platelets, liver injury, or low sodium—early, before they cause severe symptoms.

faqs.q: What serious warning signs should I watch for?
faqs.a: Seek urgent medical help for any new painful or widespread rash, blisters, skin peeling, fever, mouth sores, severe sore throat, repeated infections, unexplained bruising, yellowing of your eyes or skin, extreme fatigue, confusion, or seizures. These can signal rare but life-threatening reactions involving your skin, blood, liver, or sodium level.

faqs.q: What is HLA-B*1502 and why might testing be recommended?
faqs.a: HLA-B*1502 is a genetic marker found mainly in people of South and East Asian ancestry (such as Han Chinese, Thai, Malaysian, Indian, or Vietnamese backgrounds). Having this marker greatly increases the risk of a severe, potentially life-threatening skin reaction (Stevens–Johnson syndrome or toxic epidermal necrolysis) with carbamazepine. If your ancestry suggests a higher risk, your clinician may recommend a one-time blood test before starting the medicine. If the test is positive, a different mood stabilizer is usually chosen.

faqs.q: Can I drink alcohol while taking carbamazepine?
faqs.a: Alcohol and carbamazepine both slow down the brain. Together, they can greatly increase drowsiness, dizziness, poor coordination, and risk of falls or accidents. Alcohol can also destabilize mood. Most clinicians recommend avoiding or strictly limiting alcohol while on carbamazepine, especially when your dose is changing.

Yes. Carbamazepine speeds up the breakdown of the hormones in many birth control pills, patches, and rings, which can make them less effective and increase the risk of unplanned pregnancy. If pregnancy is possible, talk with your prescriber about using a non-hormonal method (such as a copper IUD or condoms) or another contraceptive option that is less affected by enzyme-inducing medications.

Carbamazepine is associated with a higher risk of certain birth defects, but uncontrolled bipolar disorder or seizures also carry serious risks to you and the baby. If you are pregnant or planning a pregnancy, do not stop carbamazepine suddenly on your own. Instead, talk with your psychiatrist and obstetric provider about the risks and benefits, possible alternatives, folic acid supplementation, and how you and the fetus will be monitored if you stay on the medicine.

faqs.q: Can I breastfeed while taking carbamazepine?
faqs.a: Carbamazepine does enter breast milk, but most studies have not shown long-term harm to children who were breastfed while their parent was on the drug. Some infants have had sedation, feeding problems, or changes in liver tests. If you breastfeed while taking carbamazepine, your baby’s pediatrician should keep an eye on sleepiness, feeding, weight gain, jaundice, and development, and may occasionally order blood tests if there are concerns.

faqs.q: What should I do if I miss a dose?
faqs.a: If you remember fairly soon after your usual time, you can usually take the missed dose. If it’s close to your next scheduled dose, skip the missed one and just take the next dose at the usual time—don’t double up. If you miss several doses in a row, your carbamazepine level can fall, and mood or seizures may destabilize, so contact your clinician for advice.

faqs.q: Can carbamazepine ever make my mood worse?
faqs.a: Carbamazepine aims to stabilize mood, but like other antiseizure medications it can sometimes be associated with new or worsening depression, anxiety, irritability, or suicidal thoughts. It can also cause cognitive slowing that some people experience as emotional “numbness.” If you notice concerning mood changes, let your clinician know promptly so your treatment plan can be reviewed.

faqs.q: Is carbamazepine a first-line treatment for bipolar disorder?
faqs.a: No. For most people with bipolar disorder, first-line medications for acute mania and long-term prevention include lithium, valproate, and atypical antipsychotics. Carbamazepine is typically used as an alternative when those options are not suitable or have failed, or when someone has responded particularly well to carbamazepine in the past. Because of its interaction profile and potential for serious side effects, it is best used with close monitoring by clinicians who are familiar with mood stabilizers.
